title: Family: the people class and plurals that swap the head of the word
goal: Name family members, introduce people, form plurals by swapping the prefix, and say "have" without using a verb at all.
bekal: form the plural of the people class: *mtoto → watoto*, *mwalimu → walimu*
match an adjective to its class: *mtoto mdogo → watoto wadogo*
say have and don't have with *nina*, *una*, *ana* — and *sina*, *huna*, *hana*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Picha ya familia
dialogs.intro: Late afternoon on the veranda. Amina shows Budi the photos on her phone.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Angalia, hii ni picha ya familia yangu.
lines.id: Look, this is a photo of my family.
lines.literal: look, this is picture of family of-me.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Familia yako ni kubwa! Hawa ni nani?
lines.id: Your family is big! Who are these people?
lines.literal: family of-you is big! these-people are who?

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Huyu ni baba yangu, na huyu ni mama yangu.
lines.id: This is my father, and this is my mother.
lines.literal: this-person is father of-me, and this-person is mother of-me.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Baba yako ni mrefu sana! Yeye ni mwalimu?
lines.id: Your father is very tall! Is he a teacher?
lines.literal: father of-you is tall very! he is teacher?

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Hapana, yeye ni daktari. Mama yangu ni mwalimu.
lines.id: No, he's a doctor. My mother is the teacher.
lines.literal: no, he is doctor. mother of-me is teacher.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Na hawa watoto wadogo ni nani?
lines.id: And who are these little children?
lines.literal: and these-people children small-ones are who?

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Hao ni watoto wa kaka yangu. Ana watoto watatu.
lines.id: They're my brother's children. He has three children.
lines.literal: those-people are children of brother of-me. he-has children three.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Hapana, sina. Sina mume bado. Na wewe je?
lines.id: No, I don't. I don't have a husband yet. And you?
lines.literal: no, I-don't-have. I-don't-have husband yet. and you how?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Mimi nina dada mmoja tu. Yeye ni mwanafunzi.
lines.id: I only have one sister. She's a student.
lines.literal: I I-have sister one only. she is student.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Familia yako ni ndogo, lakini nzuri. Karibu nyumbani kwetu!
lines.id: Your family is small, but nice. Come visit our house!
lines.literal: family of-you is small, but good. welcome at-home of-us!

notes: **Hii, huyu, hawa — there are many words for "this".** Swahili picks the form of "this" according to the noun class: *huyu* for one person, *hawa* for several people, *hii* for things like *picha* and *familia*. For now learn the three as whole words; the full table follows in unit 6.

**Ya in picha ya familia means "of".** Its form follows the class of the noun before it: *picha ya familia* (picture of the family), but *watoto wa kaka* (children of the brother). Like the possessives, it changes clothes — and that is the heart of this language.

**Je? at the end of a sentence means "how?".** *Na wewe je?* is how you toss the same question back at your partner without repeating it. A tiny piece that makes your conversation sound alive at once.
**Bado means "not yet" and goes at the end.** *Sina mume bado* = "I don't have a husband yet". On its own, *Bado* is also a complete answer to "already?" — it means "not yet".

**Dada and kaka aren't only for siblings.** Both are used to address people of your own age: *dada* for women, *kaka* for men, much like "sis" and "bro". For older people use *mama* and *baba* — which also don't mean your actual parents.

grammars.title: The people class: plurals that swap the head of the word
body: Swahili doesn't add an ending for the plural — it **swaps the prefix**. The first class you set up is the people class: **M-** for one person, **WA-** for several.
after: Adjectives **change prefix along with their noun**, and this is the signature sound of Swahili: *mtoto mdogo* (small child) → *watoto wadogo* (small children). *mgeni mzuri* → *wageni wazuri*. *mzee mrefu* → *wazee warefu*. One sound, spreading through the whole sentence.

The six most common adjectives: **-zuri** (good, beautiful), **-baya** (bad), **-kubwa** (big), **-dogo** (small), **-refu** (tall; long), **-fupi** (short). The hyphen in front means: the class prefix goes there.

⚠️ Not every word for a person belongs to this class. *Baba*, *mama*, *dada*, *kaka*, *rafiki* and *daktari* have no *m-* prefix because they are all loanwords — their plurals are formed differently (*marafiki*, *madaktari*) or don't change at all. But they are still **treated as people** in a sentence: *baba yangu ni mrefu*, not *baba yangu ni ndefu*.

grammars.title: Having: nina, una, ana — without a verb
body: Swahili has no verb "to have". What it has is a subject prefix attached straight to *na* ("with") — literally "I with", "you with".
after: Look at the negative forms: **si-**, **hu-**, **ha-**, **hatu-**, **ham-**, **hawa-**. These six prefixes will come back exactly the same in unit 4 to negate every verb in Swahili. Memorizing them now puts you halfway there.
*Sina* on its own is already a complete answer to "do you have?" — it means "I don't". Likewise *hana*, *hatuna* and so on.

A "have" sentence with a number puts the number **after the noun**: *nina kaka wawili* (I have two brothers), *ana watoto watatu* (he has three children). The number changes prefix too — that's unit 5's business.

sections.title: Familia yangu — the whole household in one table

blocks.text: Swahili doesn't distinguish older and younger siblings in one word: *kaka* means brother, older or younger. If you need to specify, add *mkubwa* (big) or *mdogo* (small): *kaka mkubwa* (older brother), *dada mdogo* (younger sister).

What Swahili does distinguish is something English doesn't: **uncles on the mother's and father's side have different names**. *Mjomba* is your mother's brother; your father's brother is called *baba mdogo* or *baba mkubwa* — "little father" and "big father", depending on whether he is younger or older than your father. Likewise *shangazi* (father's sister) stands against *mama mdogo* and *mama mkubwa* (mother's sisters).

sections.title: Kazi gani? — the jobs people mention most

blocks.text: After name and origin, the third question in East Africa is almost always about work. All these words are used with *ni*: *Mimi ni mwalimu*, *Yeye ni dereva*.

Notice how many of them are built from verbs: *mfanyakazi* from *kufanya kazi* (to work), *mkulima* from *kulima* (to farm), *mvuvi* from *kuvua* (to fish), *mpishi* from *kupika* (to cook). The prefix **m-/wa-** attached to a verb root means "person who…" — a word-making machine that will save you hundreds of memorized words.
